name: Participation officer, municipality
summary: A participation officer at a mid-sized municipality describes running twelve neighbourhood tables on a new park plan. Her strongest advice is to write the project context before anything else: two paragraphs on the decision the council has to take and what residents can still change, which she says made every summary and report sharper. She tested the portal with colleagues the week before, kept one question per table, and put a phone in the middle of each table rather than collecting audio afterwards. She regrets not telling residents up front how the results would come back to them, and now sends the published report to everyone who left an email address.

chunks.text: We used it for the park plan, twelve tables across four evenings, about eighty residents in total.

The first thing I would tell anyone is to write the project context before you invite a single person. Two paragraphs: what the council actually has to decide, and what is still open. Every summary and the report came out sharper because of it.
The week before, I had six colleagues go through the portal on their own phones. We found that the welcome text was far too long and that one question was really two questions.
So one question per table, written as plainly as we could, and a phone in the middle of the table recording the whole time. We did not try to collect audio afterwards; that never works.
What I would do differently: say on the first evening how the results come back. People asked me that at every table. Now we publish the report and send it to everyone who left an email address.

name: Researcher, university
summary: A university researcher used dembrane for eight focus groups on student housing in two languages. He set the project language per session, added the place names and housing terms students use as key terms so the transcripts got them right, and switched on anonymised transcripts before the first recording because his ethics approval required it. He reads every transcript once before analysis and fixes names the transcription missed. For analysis he uses the chat in Specific Details mode with only the groups he is comparing selected, and asks for quotes he can check against the transcript rather than for conclusions.

chunks.text: Eight focus groups on student housing, half of them in Dutch and half in English, so the language setting mattered from the start.

Before the first session I added key terms: the street names, the names of the housing providers, and the slang students use for the short-stay rooms. Without that the transcripts mangled exactly the words we cared about.
Anonymised transcripts were on before anyone spoke. My ethics approval required it, and you cannot switch it on afterwards for audio you already have.
I still read every transcript once and fix the odd name. It takes twenty minutes per group and it means I trust what the chat quotes back to me.
For analysis I select just the groups I am comparing and use Specific Details. I ask for quotes I can check, not for conclusions. The conclusions are my job.

name: Facilitator, consultancy
summary: An independent facilitator who runs strategy workshops for clients explains how she closes a session with dembrane. She generates a first report during the lunch break and reads the strongest tensions back to the room in the afternoon, which she says builds more trust than anything else she does. She keeps tables to five or six people so every voice reaches the recording, and asks participants to confirm what was captured before they leave. She warns against sharing the report with the client before the room has seen it, and against long portal introductions that people skip.

chunks.text: Most of my work is one-day strategy workshops for clients, sixty to a hundred people in a room.

My trick is the lunch break. I generate a first report from the morning tables and in the afternoon I read the two or three sharpest tensions back to the room. People hear their own words and the mood changes.
Tables of five or six, never more. With eight people the quiet ones disappear, from the conversation and from the recording.
Before people leave I ask them to confirm what was captured at their table. It catches mistakes and people feel it is theirs.
Two warnings. Do not send the report to the client before the room has seen it. And keep the portal introduction to two sentences, because nobody reads more.
